title: The garden (8.12)
hookLine: take up and read, and the storm inside him goes quiet
tomorrow: who stood next to Augustine at the font?

cards: A voice drifts over a wall, a kid singing the same words again and again, the way kids do with a jingle. Augustine is under a fig tree in a garden in Milan, crying. The words are tolle lege: take up and read.

He can't place them in any children's game he knows. So he gets up, goes back to the bench where Alypius is sitting, picks up the book of Paul's letters he left there, and opens it at random. His eyes land on two verses.

teach.b: First, the verses. Romans thirteen, in the Douay-Rheims: "Let us walk honestly, as in the day: not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and impurities, not in contention and envy."
Then: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." Chambering is an old word for what goes on in bedrooms that shouldn't. It's a list of the very life Augustine kept saying not yet to.
Put on, like clothes. Paul doesn't say try harder. He says get dressed.
That's what breaks the stalemate of two wills: not a stronger push from the old self, but a new garment over it. Third, how little he read.
Augustine says he would read no further, and didn't need to. In his Latin: omnes dubitationis tenebrae diffugerunt. All the darkness of doubt fled away.
No argument closed the case. Two verses did. Fourth, what he did next.
He marks the place with a finger and, with a calm face, tells Alypius.
Alypius asks to see, reads the line after, about receiving the one who is weak in faith, and takes it for himself.
Then they go inside to tell Monica, and she is overjoyed. The scene that began with weeping under a tree ends indoors, with good news.

how: Catholics practice lectio divina, a slow, prayerful reading of a short passage of scripture; Augustine's garden is a story of one short passage, read and then put down.

games.q: you've been stuck for months on whether to quit a team. a friend sends you one sentence that lands. what does Augustine's garden suggest?
o: stop there and let it land; more reading isn't always the step.
read twenty more articles before trusting it.
wait for a voice over a wall before deciding.
games.why: Augustine read two verses, marked the place, and read no further. The case was closed by a short line, not a long argument.

practice: If you can, write one line by hand, slowly: put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ. If that line isn't yours, write one short sentence you'd like to wear like a coat. Then stop, the way Augustine did, and read no further.

wordCard.voice: The garden. Where a child's voice, a book opened at random and two verses ended Augustine's long not yet.

orig.note: Latin, Confessions 8.12: all the darkness of doubt fled away.

carryVoice: All darkness vanished, and it took two short verses, not a whole library of arguments. Until tomorrow.
